In brief

When the saccharine opening of Nausicaa gives way to a description of Gerty MacDowell, the prose briefly becomes animated by new kinds of falseness— blandishments from ads for women's products. Some of the advertisements have run in newspapers, but others come from periodicals marketed to a female readership. Two such London weeklies are named in the chapter: the Lady's Pictorial, a magazine that touted itself as a "First Class medium for all advertisements appealing to Ladies," and The Princess's Novelettes, which published one "complete story" per issue but wedged the story between ads. The ads that Joyce references in these paragraphs are for products said, hyperbolically and often fraudulently, to increase beauty, promote health, and remedy physical deficiencies.

At more length

Gerty's eyes, we learn, are "set off by lustrous lashes and dark expressive brows. Time was when those brows were not so silkily seductive. It was Madame Vera Verity, directress of the Woman Beautiful page of the Princess Novelette, who had first advised her to try eyebrowleine which gave that haunting expression to the eyes, so becoming in leaders of fashion, and she had never regretted it." Slote, Mamigonian, and Turner note that Joyce invented the Woman Beautiful page and took the name Vera Verity from "a 'second-rate actress' and con artist in the short story 'Admired by All' by R. M. Niederhauser." But The Princess Novelettes did have an "advice to correspondents" page, and Eyebrowlin was an English brand of "eyelash and eyebrow grower." The ad reproduced here, first published ca. 1916, claimed that Eyebrowlin is "used by leaders of fashion" and "produces that fascinating expression which is becoming to ladies." In a JJON note Harald Beck observes that its brand name is meant to evoke "eyebrow line" and that Joyce wrote -line in the Rosenbach manuscript. The French-sounding -eine could be his choice his choice to make the product sound more elegant, or it could be simply a printer's mistake.

In the next sentence, still echoing phrases encountered in ads, Gerty thinks, "Then there was blushing scientifically cured and how to be tall increase your height and you have a beautiful face but your nose? That would suit Mrs Dignam because she had a button one." Slote's team cites a 1918 English ad promising "Blushing Cured in 7 Days. My System of Nerve Culture cures the awkward and inconvenient habit of blushing"—a claim sure to interest the often-red Gerty—and American ads of 1903 and 1905 promoting the height-increasing program of Leo Minges, founder of the Cartilage Company in Rochester, New York. One ad claims that "Mr Minges is to short men and women what the great wizard Edison is to electricity." (He was arrested for fraud in 1913.) Ads in other American papers starting in about 1915 promoted a "nose-shaper" made in New York by M. Trilety, a "Face Specialist." Designed to be "worn at night," it promised to make people more popular by radically reshaping their noses "without operation." Those ads led with the hook, "You have a beautiful face but your nose?" The one reproduced here offers a "before" picture of a button nose like Mrs. Dignam's.

Gerty prides herself on her "neat blouse of electric blue selftinted by dolly dyes (because it was expected in the Lady's Pictorial that electric blue would be worn)." The Lady's Pictorial encouraged middle-class women to believe that dressing in accordance with its suggestions would enable them to participate in the elegant styles of the upper classes. Gerty has used the trademarked dyes sold by an English firm to obtain the "electric blue" color recommended by this journal. William Edge and Sons built their first factory in Bolton, Lancashire in the 1870s, and later opened warehouses and offices in London, Dublin, Belfast, Glasgow, New York, and Melbourne. The company marketed "Dolly fast dyes," "Dolly blue" (for restoring whiteness to garments), and the "Dolly tints" echoed in Gerty's language.

The first paragraph devoted to Gerty mentions that "those iron jelloids she had been taking of late had done her a world of good." These iron supplements encapsulated in gelatine lozenges were supposed to cure anemia and other forms of what she calls "that tired feeling." In a 16 July 1915 London Times ad the Jelloid Company of London promised that they would "enrich the blood—restore energy." Gerty thinks that they are "much better than the Widow Welch's female pills and she was much better of those discharges she used to get." This other patent medicine, also manufactured in London, combined iron with sulfur. Its ads claimed that it would cure "female obstructions," and it seems that Gerty has tried them because of vaginal "discharges." But the product was widely used as an abortifacient, and the ads promising to remove obstructions hinted at this function—the pills would get the menstrual blood flowing again by removing an embryo.

A final product mentioned in this paragraph, the "queen of ointments," could refer to several different skin creams, one of them a French product called La Reine des Crèmes, manufactured by the Parisian firm Fossard-Lemaire. The brand name is well suited to appeal to Gerty, who thinks constantly of the Blessed Virgin ("Queen of angels, queen of patriarchs, queen of prophets, of all saints [...] queen of the most holy rosary"), and who possesses "an innate refinement, a languid queenly hauteur." Slote, Mamigonian, and Turner note that this phrase is the title of chapter 30 of The Lamplighter and was commonly used in other 19th century sentimental novels, one of them "Mrs Gore's The Diamond and the Pearl (1849): 'Lady De Hauteford was a woman who affected queenly hauteur' (vol. 3, p. 71)." It works also with the Odyssean reference to Nausicaa as a princess. 

Occasional references to other commercial advertisements are scattered around the first part of Nausicaa, but the ones clustered in Gerty's first few paragraphs are both obtrusive and cohesive. They conspire to define her as a person whose sense of self has been significantly shaped by marketing departments—exactly as those entities would have it. The Lady's Pictorial feeds her conviction that she should have been born a member of the landed gentry. The queen of ointments encourages her to model herself on the Queen of Heaven. Eyebrowlin gives her eyes that "haunting expression" that makes "leaders of fashion" so compelling. Gerty may not aspire to increase her height or change the shape of her nose, but the very fact that she recalls ads promising those things indicates that she accepts their premise:

In this age attention to your appearance is an absolute necessity if you expect to make the most out of life. Not only should you wish to appear as attractive as possible for your own self-satisfaction, which is alone well worth your efforts, but you will find the world in general judging you greatly, if not wholly, by your "looks," therefore it pays to look your best at all times. Permit no one to see you looking otherwise; it will injure your welfare! Upon the impression you constantly make rests the failure or success of your life. 

To the extent that one likes Gerty, one must hope that as she grows older she will discern the falsity of this claim and find other standards for measuring the success or failure of her life. Still, she has made herself into something, and Bloom's response confirms the ravishing effect. The poignancy of his reflection on what will become of Woman Beautiful shows what Gerty is struggling against: "Sad however because it lasts only a few years till they settle down to potwalloping and papa's pants will soon fit Willy and fullers' earth for the baby when they hold him out to do ah ah."

John Hunt 2026
